title: Caching layers and invalidation

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Caching layers and invalidation

children.text: Caching is the cheapest performance win and the most common source of confusing bugs. Decide where it lives and what invalidates it before you add it.
What this lesson covers
Place caches at the edge, application, or data layer
Choose a write strategy and an eviction policy
Plan invalidation before you plan the cache
This lesson sits in Core Building Blocks, part of System Design Foundations. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Place caches at the edge, application, or data layer
Choose a write strategy and an eviction policy
Plan invalidation before you plan the cache
proTip: Design the invalidation path first. A cache you cannot invalidate is a bug with a latency benefit.

title: Queues and asynchronous work

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Queues and asynchronous work

children.text: A queue decouples producers from consumers and absorbs bursts. The cost is that you now have to think about ordering, retries, and duplicates.
What this lesson covers
Move slow work out of the request path
Handle retries, dead letters, and duplicate delivery
Reason about ordering guarantees you actually have

keyPoints: Move slow work out of the request path
Handle retries, dead letters, and duplicate delivery
Reason about ordering guarantees you actually have

title: Sharding and partitioning

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Sharding and partitioning

title: Replication and read scaling

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Replication and read scaling

children.text: Replicas give you read capacity and failover. They also give you a window where a follower answers with data that is slightly out of date.
What this lesson covers

Plan and rehearse failover

title: Consistency models and CAP

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Consistency models and CAP

children.text: When the network partitions you choose consistency or availability. Most real systems pick a different answer per operation.
What this lesson covers
Place a system on the consistency spectrum
Choose guarantees per operation, not per database
Explain the user-visible effect of eventual consistency
This lesson sits in Data at Scale, part of System Design Foundations. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Place a system on the consistency spectrum
Choose guarantees per operation, not per database
Explain the user-visible effect of eventual consistency
proTip: Ask what the user sees when a read is stale. That answer picks your consistency model faster than any theorem.

title: REST and GraphQL trade-offs

title: Idempotency and safe retries

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Idempotency and safe retries

children.text: Any request can be delivered twice. An idempotency key lets the second delivery return the first result instead of charging the card again.
What this lesson covers
Make write endpoints safe to retry
Accept and store idempotency keys
Retry with backoff and jitter, not in lockstep
This lesson sits in API Design at Scale, part of System Design Foundations. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Make write endpoints safe to retry
Accept and store idempotency keys
Retry with backoff and jitter, not in lockstep
proTip: Retries without jitter turn one blip into a synchronised stampede.

title: Timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers

children.text: A dependency that hangs is worse than one that fails. Timeouts convert hanging into failing, and circuit breakers stop failure spreading.
What this lesson covers
Set timeouts on every outbound call
Break the circuit when a dependency is clearly down
Degrade gracefully instead of cascading
